opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about quite a lot. For me, success isn't really about a single paper or a particular title. It's more about whether the things I build actually end up being useful to other people — whether they enable others to do work they couldn't have done before.

When I started working on projects like XGBoost, and later TVM and machine learning systems more broadly, the most rewarding moments weren't when we published something. They were when I'd hear from someone I'd never met — a data scientist at a company, a student in another country — saying they used the tool to solve their problem or win a competition. That's when you realize the work has taken on a life of its own, beyond you.

So I'd say the contribution I care about is building foundations. In research, especially in systems, much of the impact is indirect. You're building the infrastructure that lets other people build the exciting things on top. If, years from now, people are running models more efficiently on all kinds of devices, and part of that traces back to ideas or open-source tools our community created, I would consider that success.

There's also a community side. Open source taught me that the best things are rarely built by one person. Success also means growing an ecosystem — bringing in contributors, helping students grow into independent researchers, and seeing them go off and do things much bigger than what I could do alone.

And finally, I try to keep it a bit personal and long-term. I ask myself whether I'm working on problems I genuinely believe matter, and whether I'm still learning. If I keep doing that, and the work keeps being useful to people, then I feel I'm on the right path, regardless of any particular external measure.

r001.rationale: He defines success as building technology that becomes useful to others and enables work they could not do before, describing tools and infrastructure that let people build on his work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. For me, success is really about building things that lower the barrier for other people. I have spent most of my career building machine learning systems like XGBoost, TVM, and more recently MLC LLM, and the common thread is that I care less about a single paper or benchmark result and more about whether the tool actually ends up in the hands of people who can do something with it.

When I was working on XGBoost, I never imagined it would become the default tool for so many Kaggle competitions and production systems. What made that meaningful was not the citation count. It was seeing people who are not machine learning researchers, people in finance, biology, or small startups, pick it up and solve problems I would never have thought of. That is the kind of leverage I find exciting. One piece of well-designed infrastructure can multiply the impact of thousands of other people.

So I think about contribution in terms of layers. There is the research layer, where you push the frontier of what is possible. There is the systems layer, where you make that frontier efficient and reliable. And then there is the open source and community layer, where you make it accessible, so that the capability does not stay locked inside a few big companies. I believe the most durable progress happens when all three move together. Right now with large language models, for example, the frontier is moving fast, but if running those models requires a data center, most of the world is excluded. Part of what drives our work on machine learning compilation is the idea that a capable model should be able to run on your laptop or your phone, and that people everywhere should be able to build on top of it.

The other thing I would say is that I measure success partly by the people. I am a professor, and a lot of my students and collaborators have gone on to build their own projects and communities. If the ideas and the way of thinking about problems propagate beyond what I personally build, that feels more like real contribution than anything I can put on a resume.

So to summarize: success means that the systems I help create become useful, open, and widely adopted, and that they enable others to create things I could not have created myself.

r001.rationale: He describes success as building technology that lowers barriers, reaches people across fields, and enables them to solve problems and create things of their own.

astra-6.text:
For me, success is about enabling other people to do things they couldn’t do before. If something I build helps someone explore an idea, solve a problem, or create something useful, that’s a meaningful contribution.

And I think the lasting part is whether that work can grow beyond me. Can other people take it in directions I never imagined? Can they contribute and make it better? I would feel successful if the answer is yes—if what started as my contribution becomes something much larger through other people’s efforts.

r001.rationale: The response describes enabling others through something the speaker builds, but it does not clearly identify technology as the means of influencing people.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, success means creating something that enables other people to do things they couldn’t do before. In the work I do, that might be a tool or a system that makes it easier for someone to turn an idea into reality.

You can measure that through adoption, but I think the deeper question is whether the work continues to be useful beyond your own involvement. Can other people build on it, improve it, and take it in directions you hadn’t imagined? If that happens, then your contribution becomes much bigger than what you could accomplish alone. That’s the kind of success I would hope for.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes success as creating tools or systems that enable others to act, build on the work, and extend its impact, communicating influence through technology.
